canonical: I’m buying notebooks and pens with a fixed budget. Show me all the combinations I can afford.
paraphrases: Show every basket of notebooks and pens that fits my budget.
Help me see which whole notebooks and pens I can afford together.
followups: Keep item prices fixed and make the budget 80.
Require at least two notebooks.
invalid: Let me buy negative quantities and still call the basket affordable.

canonical: Why does one really expensive house make the average house price look so high?
paraphrases: Show how a luxury home changes average prices compared with the middle price.
Why is the mean home price affected more than the median by one very costly house?
followups: Change the last house to 1000 and keep the other six prices.
Add an eighth house priced 130 and keep every existing house.
invalid: Remove every house and say the average price is zero.

canonical: Can two classes have the same average score but very different results? Show me.
paraphrases: Compare two classes whose average is 70 but whose scores are spread differently.
Can identical mean scores hide different amounts of variation?
followups: Spread the second class symmetrically with spacing 5 points.
Use sample standard deviation instead of population deviation.
invalid: Report a defined sample standard deviation for one student.

canonical: Why might a survey of 20 people give a different answer from a survey of 500?
paraphrases: Compare the variability of surveys of 20 and 500 people.
Why do small random surveys fluctuate more than large ones?
followups: Use 500 people per survey and keep the population at 60%.
Use biased selection at 80% while keeping population truth at 60%.
invalid: Promise every larger sample is closer to the population.

canonical: Plot study hours against exam scores and let me see what happens when one student doesn’t follow the trend.
paraphrases: Let me change one student on a study-time versus test-score scatterplot.
Show how an unusual exam score changes a fitted study-hours trend.
followups: Change only the last student score to 10.
Add a student with ID student-6, 10 study hours and a score of 40.
invalid: Make all study hours identical and still give a unique least-squares slope.

canonical: If I already know the marble is blue, how does that change the chance it came from the first bag?
paraphrases: Seeing a blue marble, how likely was the first bag its source?
Compare the original bag chance with the chance after learning the marble is blue.
followups: Set the first bag selection probability to 20% and keep both contents.
Remove all blue marbles from both bags while keeping their red contents.
invalid: Compute a defined probability given blue when blue is impossible.

canonical: Why is choosing three teammates different from choosing first, second, and third place?
paraphrases: Compare picking a team of three with awarding three ordered places.
How does counting a three-person team differ from a three-place podium?
followups: Switch to podium order and keep five people and three selections.
Choose two people from the same five.
invalid: Choose six distinct people from five without replacement.

canonical: Show me where each loan payment goes and what changes if I pay a little extra every month.
paraphrases: Compare a normal fixed-rate loan with extra principal payments.
Show the interest and principal parts of monthly payments and early payoff.
followups: Add 50 currency units extra per month, preserving principal, rate and term.
Compare a second independent loan at zero annual interest with the same principal and term.
invalid: Include variable interest rates and missed payments in this fixed-rate model.

canonical: If this graph shows how far a car has travelled, how do I tell how fast it’s going at one exact moment?
paraphrases: Show how average car velocity approaches the velocity at one instant.
Shrink the time interval on a position curve and compare secant and tangent slopes.
followups: Use h=0.1 seconds and keep selected time 3 seconds.
Use the reversing motion preset while keeping t=3 and h=0.1.
invalid: Calculate the secant by dividing by h=0.

canonical: If a tap runs faster and slower over time, how can I work out how much water ended up in the tank?
paraphrases: Find the water collected under a changing tap flow-rate curve.
Show how adding small flow rectangles estimates tank inflow over time.
followups: Use right-endpoint rectangles while keeping the three-minute interval and flow.
Add a knot at one minute with rate four litres per minute, retaining the endpoint knots.
invalid: Keep all water in a tank whose capacity is below the computed inflow.
